items.title: Cognitive load theory shapes instructional design
items.claim: John Sweller's cognitive load theory (1988 onwards) distinguishes three types of load. Which design principle follows directly?

options.text: Always make instructions as long as possible

Minimise extraneous load (poor design) and manage intrinsic load (task complexity) so working memory can devote capacity to germane load (schema formation) — worked examples for novices, problem-solving for experts (expertise reversal effect)

items.reveal_title: Working memory is the bottleneck for learning
items.reveal:
Sweller's theory builds on Miller's 7+/-2 and Baddeley's working memory. Educational applications include worked-example effect (better than problem-solving for novices), modality effect (combining visual + auditory exceeds visual alone), redundancy effect (repeating information harms learning).

David Geary distinguishes 'biologically primary' knowledge (language, faces) that we acquire effortlessly from 'biologically secondary' (reading, algebra) that requires designed instruction. The theory has reshaped UK curriculum guidance (EEF 2018, Ofsted 2019).
items.why: Teaching that ignores working memory limits — long instructions, complex diagrams, novice problem-solving — is measurably less effective. CLT puts a constraint into instructional design.

items.title: The multi-store model was too simple for working memory
items.claim: Atkinson and Shiffrin's 1968 multi-store model split memory into sensory, short-term and long-term stores. What replaced its account of short-term memory?

options.text: Nothing — the multi-store model is unchanged

Baddeley and Hitch's 1974 working memory model — a central executive coordinating a phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad and (later) episodic buffer — better fitted evidence that STM is not a single unitary store

items.reveal:
Patients with impaired STM (e.g., KF, studied by Shallice and Warrington 1970) could nonetheless retain visual information and form new long-term memories — evidence STM had components. Baddeley and Hitch (1974) proposed a multi-component working memory. The episodic buffer was added by Baddeley in 2000.

The multi-store model is still taught as a stepping stone but is superseded for STM specifically.
items.why: Models that fit the original data often fail later, more specific data. Working memory's multiple components matter for education, clinical assessment and cognitive neuroscience.

items.title: Long-term memory is not one system
items.claim: Endel Tulving distinguished episodic and semantic memory. What is the key difference?

options.text: Episodic stores facts; semantic stores experiences

Episodic memory is autobiographical and time-stamped (your breakfast this morning); semantic is general knowledge (London is the UK capital). Procedural memory (how to ride a bike) is a third, separate system

items.reveal:
Patient HM (Henry Molaison) could not form new episodic memories after his 1953 surgery but retained semantic knowledge from before the operation and could acquire new procedural skills (motor mirror-tracing).

Neuroimaging (Tulving, Nyberg, Cabeza 2000s) supports differential activation: hippocampus crucial for episodic; widespread cortical networks for semantic; basal ganglia/cerebellum for procedural. Different forms of dementia (semantic dementia vs Alzheimer's) damage these systems differently.
items.why: Treating memory as a single capacity misses clinically and educationally important distinctions. Memory loss patterns reveal architecture.
